en: The Sūtra on Seeking Desire, translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmakṣema of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying in the Veṇuvana (Bamboo Grove) at the Kalandakanivāpa (Squirrels’ Feeding Place) in Rājagṛha.
Measuring the Deer Park,
at that time the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones!..."
There are four kinds of persons in the world who can be known by their outward appearance. What are the four?
These, O worthy ones!
There may be someone who has internal desire, yet does not know, as it truly is, that he has internal desire.
Venerable friends!
There may be someone who has internal desire, and knows, as it truly is, that he has internal desire.
"Venerable friends!
There may be a person who has no internal desire for seeking, yet he does not know, as it truly is, that he has no internal desire for seeking.
Venerable friends!"
There may be someone who has no internal seeking or desire; that he has no internal seeking or desire, he knows as it truly is.

But, worthy friends, if there is another person who has internal seeking or desire, yet does not know that he has internal seeking or desire as it truly is—I say that such a person is the most base and evil of men.
"Venerable friends!
Suppose there is a person who has internal desires; when that person has internal desires and knows them as they truly are, I say that this person is the most excellent among men."
"Venerable friends!

Suppose there is a person who has no internal seeking-desire, yet because he does not know that lack of internal seeking-desire as it truly is, I say that this person is the most base and evil of men."
"Venerable friends!
Suppose there is a person who is without internal seeking; that he is without internal seeking, he knows as it truly is. Of such a person, I say that he is the most excellent of men."

At that time, a certain bhikkhu rose from his seat, adjusted his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Venerable Sāriputta, and addressed the Venerable Sāriputta, saying: "How is it, Venerable Sāriputta?"
For what cause and for what reason, when these two former types of persons both possess desire and both possess attachment, is one described as base and evil while the other is described as supreme?

Furthermore, by what cause and by what condition are these latter two types of persons both free from seeking desire and both free from attachment, yet one is described as base and evil, while the other is described as supreme?
"Venerable friends!

Suppose there is a person who has internal longing, and being possessed of that internal longing, does not know it as it truly is; you should know that such a person lacks joyful practice, lacks progress, and lacks diligence."
Abiding in the pursuit of sensual desires, he dies with his mind attached to those desires.
Having died with his mind attached to those desires, he does not meet a good death, nor is he reborn in a favorable realm.
Why is this? Because that seeking, desiring, and attachment of the mind has come to an end.
It is just as if, O Venerable Ones!
Suppose there is a person who, whether at a marketplace or in a guest-house, brings a copper bowl that is filthy and impure.

Having brought it, he does not wash or wipe it at the proper time, nor does he polish it at the proper time; instead, he merely leaves it among dust and dirt. In this way, that copper bowl only increases its accumulation of filth.
In this way, worthy friends!
Suppose there is a person who has internal seeking-desire (*pariyeṣaṇā*), yet he does not know that he has internal seeking-desire as it truly is.

It should be known that such a person neither delights in practice, nor proceeds in practice, nor exerts himself; he merely dwells in seeking-desire, and with his mind attached to internal seeking-desire, he passes away.
If one dies while internally seeking and clinging to desire, that death is not wholesome, nor will one be reborn in a wholesome realm.
Why is this? Because that person dies having internally sought and clung to desire.
"Venerable friends!
Suppose there is a person who internally seeks sensual desires; he knows that he internally seeks sensual desires as it truly is.
It should be known that he practices with joyful diligence, he brings those desires to rest, his mind is free from seeking desire, and he passes away without attachment."
He is without desire or craving; being unattached at the time of death, he dies well and is reborn in a favorable state. Why is this?
Because he is without desire and without attachment.
It is just as if, worthy sirs, there were a person who, being a merchant or a shopkeeper, brought a copper bowl that was stained and impure.

Having brought it, he washed it at the proper time, wiped it at the proper time, and polished it at the proper time, not leaving it among dust and dirt; this copper bowl would later become pure and bright.
In this way, worthy friends!
Suppose there is a person who has internal desires; he knows those internal desires as they truly are.
It should be known that through his practice of pleasure, progress, and diligence, those desires are abandoned; being free from the intention of desire, he passes away without attachment.
He has no intention of seeking desire; being unattached at the time of death, he dies well and is reborn in a good realm. Why is this?
Because he dies with no seeking desire and no attached mind.
"Venerable friends!
Suppose there is a person who has no internal desire for sensual pleasures, yet does not know, as it truly is, that he has no internal desire for sensual pleasures;
you should know that such a person is unable to guard his eyes, ears, mind, and mental objects."

Having failed to guard the eye, ear, mind, and mental objects while dwelling therein, the mind becomes possessed by sensual desire; being obsessed with various desires and various pursuits, one passes away with a mind so attached.
Having passed away with a mind obsessed with various desires and various pursuits, one’s death is not good and one’s rebirth is not good.
Why is this? Because their minds were attached to various desires and various pursuits at the time of death.
It is just like this, worthy ones!
Suppose there is a person who, being a merchant or a guest-house keeper, brings a pure copper bowl.

Having brought it, he does not wash it at the proper time, nor does he wipe it at the proper time, nor does he polish it at the proper time; instead, he leaves it in the dust and dirt. In this way, that copper bowl later becomes defiled and impure.
In this way, worthy ones!
Suppose there is a person who has no internal seeking or desire, yet he does not know, as it truly is, that he has no internal seeking or desire;
one should know that such a person is unable to guard his eyes, ears, mind, and mental objects.

Having failed to guard the eye, the ear, the mind, and mental phenomena, he possesses a mind of lust and a mind of defiled desire; with a mind defiled by desire and seeking, he passes away attached to such things.
Having passed away with a mind defiled by desire and seeking, and being attached to them at the time of death, his end is unwholesome and his rebirth is also unwholesome.
Why is this? Because they die with their minds attached to various desires and various pursuits.
"O worthy ones!..."
Suppose there is a person who is inwardly free from seeking; that he is inwardly free from seeking, he knows as it truly is.
It should be known that such a person is able to guard the eye, the ear, and the mind with respect to mental objects (*dharma*).

Having guarded the eye, the ear, and the mind with respect to mental objects, he is likewise without desire in his mind; being without desire and without seeking, his mind is unattached when his life comes to an end.
He dies without desire, without seeking, and with a mind free from attachment; thus his death is good and his rebirth is also good.
Why is this? Because he has died with a mind that is without seeking, without desire, and without attachment.
It is just as if, worthy sirs, there were a person who was a shopkeeper or a merchant, and he brought a pure copper bowl.

Having brought it, he washed it at the proper time, wiped it at the proper time, and polished it at the proper time, and did not leave it among dust and dirt; in this way, this bowl becomes increasingly pure and bright.
In this way, worthy friends!
That person is likewise: being without internal seeking and desire, he knows that he is without internal seeking and desire as it truly is;
you should know that he is able to guard his eyes, ears, mind, and mental objects.
Having guarded his eyes, ears, mind, and dharmas, he is free from sensual desire; he has no mixed desires or cravings, and he passes away with an unattached mind.
Having passed away with an unattached mind—free from mixed desires and mixed cravings—he is well at the end and well at birth.
Why is this? Because they pass away without being defiled by desire, without being defiled by seeking, and without attachment to existence.
This, worthy sirs, is what it means.
Based on these causes and conditions, these first two types of persons harbor desires and attachments in their minds; thus, they speak of one person as base and evil, and another as supreme.

Based on these same causes and conditions, these latter two types of persons have no internal desire and no attachment in their minds; yet they too speak of one person as base and evil, and another as supreme.

At that time, another bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes properly, joined his palms toward the Venerable Śāriputra, and addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "How is it, Venerable Śāriputra?"
"What is meant by 'seeking sensual desires'? For what reason is it called 'seeking sensual desires'?
"Venerable friends!..."
Because one seeks after immeasurable unwholesome states, it is called "seeking through desire.
Venerable friends!

There may be someone in whom the arising of seeking through desire occurs; though they have committed only a slight transgression that others do not know of, they have nonetheless committed a transgression.
Venerable friends!
You should know this possibility: that another person knows what fault you have committed and is resentful toward you because of it.
Venerable friends!
If, after becoming angry, one intends to act, there will only be unwholesomeness.
Venerable friends!
Suppose a person gives rise to a slight desire for gain and commits an offense, but speaks of it privately to others rather than in the midst of the assembly; such is the nature of that offense.
Venerable friends!

You should know this possibility: that person who has committed an offense speaks of it in the midst of the assembly rather than in private; because he speaks in the midst of the assembly, his mind becomes resentful.
Venerable friends! This is so.
Once his mind is filled with resentment, whatever he intends to do will only be unwholesome.
Venerable friends!
There may be someone who has committed an offense and wishes to speak about it to those who are equal to him, yet does not speak about the offense to those who are not equal to him.
Venerable friends!

It should be known that this is possible: that a person who has committed an offense of unequal speech, having committed such an offense of unequal speech, regards that which he has committed as being born of mental resentment.
"Venerable friends!
When that mind is filled with ill will, whatever one intends to do will be nothing but unwholesome.
Venerable friends!"
There may be someone who has a desire to arise, thinking:
"I shall sit before the World-Honored One; I shall question the World-Honored One, and he shall preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus;
let no other bhikṣu sit before the World-Honored One to question him and then preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus."
"Venerable friends!

You should know this possibility: there may be another bhikkhu sitting before the Blessed One who, having questioned the Blessed One, is able to teach the Dharma to the bhikkhus, yet that person harbors resentment in his heart."
"Venerable friends!
When the mind is filled with ill will, whatever one does will be unwholesome.
Venerable friends!"
There may be someone who has a desire arising [in them]:
"May I be the one walking in front when a bhikṣu enters a place;
may no other bhikṣu be the one walking in front when a bhikṣu enters a place."
"Venerable friends!

You should know this possibility: when a bhikkhu enters a certain place, another bhikkhu goes before him; having gone before that bhikkhu who has entered the place, yet another bhikkhu goes before that first bhikkhu—this is resentment in the mind."
"Venerable friends!
When that mind is filled with ill will, whatever one intends to do will only be unwholesome.
Venerable friends!"
There may be someone who desires birth [in a higher realm] and thinks:
"Once these bhikṣus have entered the interior, they shall sit first, receive water first, and receive the lumps of food first;
I do not wish for other bhikṣus to sit before them, receive water before them, or receive the lumps of food before them once they have entered the interior."
"Venerable friends!
It should be known that it is possible for another bhikkhu, after the bhikkhus have entered, to sit down first, receive water first, and receive the lumps of food first."
When other bhikṣus have entered and are sitting before him, receiving water first and receiving the lumps of food first, that bhikṣu becomes resentful in his mind.
Once he is resentful in his mind, whatever he intends to do will be nothing but unwholesome.
"Venerable friends!
There may arise in some a desire:

'After the bhikṣus have finished eating and put away their bowls, may I preach the Dharma to the layperson, exhorting, instructing, and so forth, and through such instruction and so forth, cause them to rejoice;'"

He does not allow other bhikṣus to do so; rather, after the bhikṣus have finished eating and put away their bowls, he himself preaches the Dharma to the lay devotees, exhorting, instructing, and so forth, providing such instruction as to bring them joy.
"Venerable friends!
You should know that it is possible for another bhikkhu to go, after the bhikkhus have finished eating and their bowls have been put away, until they are made joyful.
That other bhikkhu may indeed go, after the bhikkhus have finished eating and their bowls have been put away, until they are made joyful."
"Friends, when one’s mind is thus filled with ill will, whatever one intends to do will be nothing but unwholesome. "Friends! [he said.]
There may be someone who has a desire for gain, thinking:

"If a householder enters the park, let me be the one to converse and discuss with that householder, and not allow any other bhikṣu to converse and discuss with the householder when he enters the park."
"Venerable friends!
You should know that it is possible for another bhikkhu to feel resentment when a householder has entered the park and is engaged in conversation and discussion with [other] bhikkhus."
"Venerable friends!
When that mind is filled with ill will, whatever he intends to do will be unwholesome.
Venerable friends!"
There may be someone who gives rise to a desire for gain, thinking:
"May the king, ministers, brahmins, and householders—not just one person, but all of them—recognize me;
I do not wish for other bhikṣus to be recognized by the king, ministers, brahmins, and householders—not just one person, but all of them."
"Venerable friends!
You should know that it is possible for those other bhikkhus to be well-known to kings and great ministers, as well as to brahmins and householders—not just one person."
"Venerable friends! It is not just one person, but many other bhikkhus who are known to the king, his ministers, brahmins, and householders;
they are resentful."
Once his mind has become angry, whatever he intends to do will be unwholesome.
"Venerable friends!
There may be a person who gives rise to the desire for existence:
"May I alone receive offerings from the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen;
may no other monk receive offerings from the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen."
"Venerable friends!
It should be known that there may be other bhikṣus who receive offerings from the fourfold assembly: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās."
Those other bhikṣus receive offerings from the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—and their minds become resentful.
"Venerable friends!
When that mind is full of ill will, whatever one intends to do will be nothing but unwholesome.
Venerable friends!"
There may be someone who harbors a covetous desire, thinking:
"May I obtain robes, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick, and may other bhikṣus not obtain robes, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick."
"Virtuous ones! You should know that it is possible for other bhikṣus to obtain robes, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
When those other bhikṣus obtain robes, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he becomes resentful in his mind."
"Venerable friends!
When that mind is filled with ill will, whatever one intends to do will be nothing but unwholesome.
Venerable friends!"

Furthermore, there may be other wise fellow practitioners of the holy life who should likewise abandon these immeasurable evil and unwholesome pursuits of sensual desire, and should not engage in them.
If one associates with those who are not śramaṇas while acting as a śramaṇa;
if one associates with śramaṇas who lack wisdom while acting as a wise śramaṇa;
if one does not seek to be a senior but seeks to be a senior; if one has no meditative concentration yet claims to have it; or if one associates with the impure yet claims to be pure.
Venerable friends!
Thus, regarding those who practice the holy life with wisdom, there are such immeasurable evil and unwholesome conducts.
Knowing that one possesses such conduct, and knowing that one dwells together with those who are not true śramaṇas, one is indeed a non-śramaṇa.
Associating with śramaṇas who lack wisdom, he knows he is associating with those who lack wisdom;
he should not seek the position of elder, yet seeks the position of elder in such a manner;
there is no meditative concentration, and he knows there is no meditative concentration.
Being together with the impure, one knows it as impure.

It is just as if, noble ones, there were a person—a merchant or a traveler—who came carrying a copper bowl filled with impurities and covered its opening with another bowl; if he carried it into a crowd of people, many would see it and, desiring food and wishing to obtain it, would not know that there was impurity within.

If that gathered mass of people were brought to one place and the vessel opened, and if those who wished to eat found themselves unwilling to eat, would those who had carried it there still wish to eat from it?
In this way, worthy ones!
There are certain wise practitioners of the holy life who commit such immeasurable evils and unwholesome deeds;
they associate with those who are not śramaṇas yet act as śramaṇas, and they associate with those who are not wise śramaṇas yet act as wise śramaṇas.
They do not seek what is superior while seeking what is superior; they claim there is certainty where there is no certainty; and they speak of purity while being accompanied by impurity.
Venerable friends!
Such a person possesses these and countless other evil, unwholesome qualities toward fellow practitioners of the holy life who possess wisdom.
Knowing that one is in the company of those who are not śramaṇas, they are indeed non-śramaṇas;
knowing that one is in the company of śramaṇas who lack wisdom, they are indeed non-wisdom śramaṇas;
one should not seek the status of an elder, yet one seeks the status of an elder.
When associated with the indeterminate, it is not determinate;
when associated with the impure, it is not pure.
Venerable friends!
Thus, one should not associate with such a person, nor should one honor them, nor should one serve them.

If a bhikkhu associates with or honors such a person, or pays homage to or serves such a person, it will lead only to his loss and lack of benefit for a long night; it will result in suffering and association with the miserable realms.
Therefore, worthy ones!
One should not associate with such a person; one should not honor or serve them.
"Worthy ones! This person—""
There may be someone who, having no desire for rebirth,
thinks: "If I commit an offense, I do not wish for others to know of it," and yet commits an offense.
Venerable friends!
It should be known that this is possible: if another person has committed an offense, and others know of that offense, one’s mind harbors no resentment toward them.
Venerable friends! This is so.
When the mind is free from ill will, whatever one intends to do is only wholesome.
Venerable friends!
There may be someone who, though not harboring any desire for rebirth, commits an offense and speaks of it to others, but does not speak of the offense before the assembly.
Venerable friends!

It should be known that there is such a possibility: that when a person has committed an offense, they speak of it before the assembly rather than speaking of it privately to another; having spoken of the offense before the assembly, their mind harbors no resentment.
"Venerable friends!
When the mind is free from ill will, whatever one intends to do will be only good.
Venerable friends!"
There may be someone who, without seeking rebirth, thinks:
"If there is an offense, I shall speak of it to those who are my equals, but not to those who are not my equals.
And so, there is an offense.
Venerable friends!

It should be understood that this is the case: when a person has committed an offense, they do not speak with those who are equal to them, nor do they speak with those who are not equal to them; yet regarding the offense they have committed, they do not speak with those who are equal to them, and their mind is free from ill will.
"Venerable friends!
When the mind is free from ill will, whatever one does will be only wholesome.
Venerable friends!"
Or there may be someone who has no desire to arise [from their seat] with the thought:
"Once I am seated before the World-Honored One and have questioned the World-Honored One, the World-Honored One shall preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus;
I do not wish for another bhikṣu to be seated before the World-Honored One and question the World-Honored One, so that the World-Honored One may preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus."
"Venerable friends!
It should be known that this is possible: there may be another bhikkhu present before the World-honored One while the World-honored One is teaching the Dharma to the bhikkhus;

yet another bhikkhu may be present before the World-honored One and question the World-honored One while the World-honored One is teaching the Dharma to the bhikkhus, and his mind remains free from resentment."
"Venerable friends!
If the mind is free from ill will, whatever one intends to do will be only wholesome.
Venerable friends!"
There may be someone who has no desire for gain and thinks:
"Wherever a bhikkhu goes, he walks in front; let another bhikkhu walk in front of him.
Wherever that other bhikkhu goes, let no other bhikkhu walk in front of him."
"Venerable friends!
It should be known that there may be another bhikkhu who walks in front of the bhikkhus wherever they go.
When that other bhikkhu walks in front of the bhikkhus wherever they go, his mind is free from ill will."
"Venerable friends!
When the mind is free from ill will, whatever one intends to do will be only wholesome.
Venerable friends!"
Or there may be someone who has no desire for gain, thinking:
"Once the bhikkhu has entered the inner quarters, I shall be the first to receive water and receive the lumps of food;
let it not be that another bhikkhu, once the bhikkhu has entered the inner quarters, sits down first to receive water and receive the lumps of food."
"Venerable friends!
You should know that it is possible for another bhikkhu to enter the interior first, sit down before you, receive water and receive solid food, and yet have no ill will in his heart."
"Venerable friends!
When the mind is free from ill will, whatever one does will be only wholesome.
Venerable friends!"
There may be someone who harbors no desire for gain, thinking:
"After the bhikṣus have finished eating and withdrawn their bowls, let me be the one to teach, instruct, and exhort the layperson, and through such instruction and so forth, bring them to joy;
do not let another bhikṣu, after the bhikṣus have finished eating and withdrawn their bowls, teach, instruct, and exhort the layperson, and through such instruction and so forth, bring them to joy."
"Venerable friends!

It should be known that it is possible for another bhikkhu, after the bhikkhus have finished eating and withdrawn their bowls, to teach the Dharma to a householder, exhorting, instructing, and thoroughly teaching him so as to gladden him, while his mind remains free from ill will."
"Venerable friends!
Once one is free from ill will, whatever one intends to do will be only wholesome.
This, venerable friends!"
Or there may be someone who harbors no desire for gain, thinking:
"Once the householder has entered the park, let me converse with him;
do not let another bhikkhu converse with him once he has entered the park."
"Venerable friends!

It should be known that there may be another bhikkhu who, when laypeople have entered the garden and are conversing together, and while other bhikkhus and laypeople have entered the garden and are conversing together, does not feel resentment in his mind."
"Venerable friends!
When that mind is free from ill will, whatever one intends to do will be only wholesome.
Venerable friends!"
Or there may be a person who gives rise to no desire, thinking:
"Let not the king, ministers, brahmins, and householders recognize me alone;
let not other bhikṣus be recognized by the king, ministers, brahmins, and householders."
"Virtuous ones! You should know that it is possible for there to be another bhikkhu who is recognized by kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders—
not just one person— and that this other bhikkhu, being recognized by kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders— not just one person— has no ill will in his heart."
"Venerable friends!
When that mind is free from ill will, whatever one intends to do will be only wholesome.
Venerable friends!"
There may be someone who gives rise to a desire without seeking it:

"May I receive offerings from the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; may no other bhikṣu receive offerings from the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās."
"Venerable friends!
It should be known that there may be another bhikkhu who receives offerings from the fourfold assembly—bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—and yet his mind remains free from ill will."
"Venerable friends!
When the mind is free from ill will, whatever one intends to do will be only wholesome.
Venerable friends!"
Or there may be someone who gives rise to a desire without seeking it, thinking:
"May I obtain robes, bedding, seats, and medicine for the sick, but may other bhikṣus not obtain robes, bedding, seats, and medicine for the sick."
"Venerable friends!
You should know that it is possible for other bhikṣus to obtain robes, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick,
while other bhikṣus likewise obtain robes, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick, and yet one feels no resentment in one's heart."
"Venerable friends!
When the mind is free from ill will, whatever one intends to do will be only wholesome.
Venerable friends!"

In this way, that person, toward those wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life who delight in the practice of immeasurable wholesome dharmas, if he does not recognize them as being together with śramaṇas, speaks of them as non-śramaṇas; if they are together with wise śramaṇas, he speaks of them as non-wise śramaṇas; if they are together with elders, he speaks of them as not being together with elders; if they are together with meditative concentration, he speaks of them as being without concentration; and if they are together with purity, he speaks of them as being impure.
In this way, worthy sirs!

There may be someone who, regarding a wise fellow practitioner of the holy life, understands all such immeasurable wholesome practices; he understands that he is living with a śramaṇa, that he is living with a wise śramaṇa, that he is living with one established in concentration, and that he is living with one established in purity.

It is just as if, worthy sirs, there were a merchant or a peddler who came carrying a copper bowl filled with various kinds of food and drink of diverse flavors, and having covered it with another bowl, he carried it into a gathering of people. When many people saw it, they did not wish to eat it nor desired to obtain it; knowing it to be something else, they said:
"This is merely an old vessel; this is merely an old vessel."

Having brought it into the midst of a great multitude, he opened the vessel; those who did not wish to eat it then desired to eat it—was it not the case that those who had seen it previously did not wish to eat it?
In this way, worthy ones!

There may be someone who, regarding a wise fellow practitioner of the holy life, does not recognize such immeasurable wholesome conducts. While in the company of a śramaṇa, he says he is not a śramaṇa; while in the company of a wise śramaṇa, he says he is not a wise śramaṇa; while in the company of a senior elder, he says he is not a senior elder; while in the company of one in meditative concentration, he says he is not in concentration; and while in the company of one who is pure, he says he is not pure.
In this way, venerable friends!

There may be a person who, regarding fellow practitioners of the holy life who possess immeasurable wholesome conduct, subsequently recognizes that those who are with a śramaṇa are indeed śramaṇas, that those who are with a wise śramaṇa are indeed wise śramaṇas, that those who are with an elder are indeed elders, that those who are with one in meditative concentration are indeed in concentration, and that those who are with one in purity are indeed pure.
In this way, worthy friends!

This person should be honored, served, and venerated; monks should associate with him. Those who honor what is to be honored, those who serve those who should be served, and those who constantly practice what should be constantly practiced—these will bring only benefit and happiness for a long night.
"Therefore, worthy ones! Such a person as this should be approached, honored, and served.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was also present in the assembly, and he said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
“Venerable Śāriputra!
I wish to speak a parable; shall I speak it? “You may speak.”
"You, worthy Maudgalyāyana! Venerable Śāriputra, formerly at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, Venerable Śāriputra!"
Rising early in the morning and putting on my robes, I took my bowl and went to Rājagṛha to beg for alms.
While wandering through Rājagṛha for alms, I arrived at the house of a master craftsman; there I saw Anāthapiṇḍada’s son staying in the master’s house, working on a wagon axle.
That son of Pūrṇa, being in the house of a master craftsman, gave rise to this thought:
"If this master craftsman takes this axle and planes it smooth in this spot, then this obstruction of the axle will be removed."

Then, while the son of the one free from conceptual thought was working at the house of a master craftsman, such a thought arose within him; and that master craftsman, according to his thought, proceeded to chop and mend the axle of a chariot with an axe.
At that time, Amanusya Pūrṇaputra spoke these words:

"This master craftsman has understood my intention and taken this axle; he has trimmed and treated it according to its original state, so that this axle will serve to increase [the vehicle's utility] without any hindrance."
"Thus it is, Venerable Śāriputra!

That person is sycophantic, a deceiver, lacking faith and having no conviction, indolent and lacking diligence, with a distracted mind and no concentration, possessing evil wisdom and mental confusion, with unstable faculties, lax in his observance of the precepts, and unable to discern the conduct of a śramaṇa."
Then the Venerable Śāriputra, knowing his thoughts, gave him this explanation: "Venerable Śāriputra, that person is free from flattery and deceit;

he is not a man of illusion. He possesses faith and joyful confidence, practices with diligence, maintains constant concentration of mind, trains in wisdom, honors the precepts, and is highly discerning regarding the conduct of a śramaṇa."
Having heard the Dharma taught by the Venerable Śāriputra, he received it with both mouth and mind as if drinking something refreshing or eating something delicious.
It was just so, Venerable Śāriputra!

If there is a daughter of a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a householder, or a craftsman who has bathed, applied perfumes, and put on pure white garments, and someone, with a mind of compassion and a desire to benefit and bring her peace and security, takes a garland of *utpala* flowers, a garland of *campaka* flowers, a garland of *vārṣika* flowers, or a garland of *atimuktaka* flowers and offers it to her, she receives it with both hands and places it upon her own head.
Thus it is, Venerable Śāriputra!

There may be someone who is neither flattering nor deceitful, who does not lack faith but possesses faith, who is able to practice diligence with a mind constantly concentrated, who possesses wisdom and reverently trains in the precepts, and who trains extensively in the various aspects of the ascetic life.
Having heard the Dharma from the Venerable Śāriputra, he was as if drinking something refreshing and as if eating something delicious; his mouth and mind were likewise so.
"How truly marvelous is this Venerable Śāriputra! he exclaimed.
Furthermore, the Venerable Śāriputra, for the sake of his fellow practitioners of the holy life, eliminates their unwholesome states and establishes them in the wholesome.
Excellent, worthy one!
You are a true person.
Having thus each spoken according to their own inclinations and taken their pleasure [in the teaching], they rose from their seats and returned to their respective abodes.
This concludes the *Buddhabhāṣita-kāmacchanda-sūtra*.
